blocks.content: Locks and semaphores are two of the most commonly used synchronization primitives in concurrent programming. At first glance, they appear very similar because both require a thread to acquire something before proceeding and release it when the work is complete.
However, they were designed to solve different problems.
A lock answers the question: "Can exactly one thread access this resource right now?"
A semaphore answers the question: "How many threads are allowed to access this resource at the same time?"
Although they can sometimes be used to achieve similar outcomes, understanding their core differences is essential for choosing the right tool and avoiding concurrency bugs.
1. What is Locks / Semaphores
A Lock (Mutex) is a synchronization mechanism that provides mutual exclusion, ensuring that only one thread can access a critical section or shared resource at a time.
A Semaphore is a synchronization mechanism that controls access to a resource using a permit counter, allowing a fixed number of threads to access the resource concurrently.
2. What a Lock Actually Guarantees
A lock, also known as a mutex (mutual exclusion), is used to protect a shared resource that must never be accessed by multiple threads simultaneously.
A lock has only two states: locked and unlocked.

When a thread acquires the lock, it becomes the exclusive owner of that lock. Any other thread attempting to acquire it must wait until the current owner releases it. As a result, only one thread can execute the protected section of code at any given moment.

The most important characteristic of a lock is ownership. The thread that acquires the lock is expected to release it later. In many implementations, attempting to release a lock from a different thread results in an error because the lock belongs to its owner.

A lock guarantees that only one thread can enter the critical section at a time. In the diagram, Thread A owns the lock and is executing inside the critical section. While A holds the lock, Threads B and C cannot enter and must wait.

When Thread A releases the lock, one of the waiting threads (either B or C) acquires the lock and becomes the new owner. This ensures that shared data is accessed by only one thread at a time, preventing race conditions and data corruption.
When A finishes and releases, the lock has room for exactly one new owner B or C whichever is next in line is let through and becomes the owner
2. What a Semaphore Actually Guarantees
A semaphore generalizes the idea of controlled access by allowing more than one thread to proceed at the same time.
Instead of having only two states, a semaphore maintains a counter known as the permit count. When a thread acquires a permit, the count decreases. When a permit is released, the count increases.
If permits are available, the thread proceeds immediately. If all permits have been consumed, the thread waits until a permit becomes available.
The key difference from a lock is that a semaphore does not track ownership. It only tracks the number of available permits.
This means the thread that releases a permit does not have to be the same thread that acquired it. From the semaphore's perspective, it is simply managing capacity rather than ownership.
A semaphore guarantees that up to N threads can access a resource simultaneously, where N is the number of permits.
In the diagram, the semaphore has 3 permits, so Thread A, Thread B, and Thread C can all run at the same time. Each thread consumes one permit when it starts.
Once all 3 permits are in use, the permit count becomes 0. When Thread D tries to acquire a permit, it cannot proceed and must wait until one of the running threads releases its permit.

When any running thread finishes and releases a permit, the semaphore wakes a waiting thread, allowing it to continue. Unlike a lock, which allows only one thread at a time, a semaphore controls how many threads can proceed concurrently.

blocks.content: This difference is easy to miss because a semaphore with 1 permit looks very similar to a mutex. In both cases, only one thread can proceed at a time. However, a mutex has ownership the thread that acquires the lock is expected to release it.

A semaphore has no ownership. Any thread can release a permit, even if it never acquired it. This difference is why mutexes are used to protect critical sections, while semaphores are used to control access to a limited resource or coordinate work between threads.
4. Why This Difference Actually Matters
The difference between locks and semaphores is not just an implementation detail it changes the kind of problems they are meant to solve.

A lock is built around ownership. When a thread acquires a lock, it becomes the owner of that lock and is responsible for releasing it later. This makes locks the perfect tool for protecting a critical section, where a thread needs exclusive access to shared data while it performs some work.

For example, if multiple threads are updating the same counter, bank balance, or configuration object, only one thread should be allowed to modify that data at a time. The thread acquires the lock, performs its work, and releases the lock when finished. The same thread handles the entire operation from start to finish.
A semaphore is built around capacity, not ownership. It does not care which thread acquired a permit or which thread releases it later. It only tracks how many permits are currently available.

This makes semaphores ideal for controlling access to a limited number of resources. Imagine a database connection pool with ten connections. A thread acquires a permit before taking a connection from the pool. Later, after the connection has been used, another thread can return it and release the permit. The semaphore simply increases its permit count and allows another waiting thread to proceed.
Because a semaphore does not track ownership, it can coordinate work across different threads. A lock cannot do that because it is tied to the thread that owns it.
In short, a lock protects a critical section, while a semaphore controls access to a limited pool of resources.

The lock example below protects a shared counter. The semaphore example limits how many database connections can be used simultaneously.
Even though the code looks similar, the intent is completely different.
With a lock, the goal is to ensure that only one thread can execute a critical section at a time.
With a semaphore, the goal is to allow a limited number of threads to proceed concurrently while preventing the total from exceeding a predefined limit.
5. Ownership and Re-entrance

A lock knows which thread owns it. Because of this, many locks support re-entrance, meaning the same thread can acquire the lock multiple times without blocking itself. This is useful when one locked method calls another method that uses the same lock.

A semaphore works differently. It does not track which thread acquired it. it only tracks the number of available permits. As a result, if a thread acquires a semaphore with one permit and tries to acquire it again before releasing it, it will block because the permit count is already zero.
In short, re-entrant locks work because locks track ownership, while semaphores cannot provide re-entrance because they only manage a counter and have no concept of ownership.

7. Common mistakes
Mistake 1: Using a Semaphore as a Mutex
A semaphore with 1 permit may look like a mutex, but it has no ownership. A wrong or extra release() can silently allow multiple threads through.
Mistake 2: Using a Lock Instead of a Semaphore
A lock allows only one thread at a time. If the requirement is "up to N threads at once" (e.g., 10 database connections), use a semaphore.
Mistake 3: Assuming a Semaphore Makes Data Thread-Safe
A semaphore only limits concurrency. It does not protect shared data from race conditions.
Mistake 4: Ignoring Re-entrance
With a non-reentrant lock, a thread that tries to acquire the same lock twice can deadlock itself. Use a re-entrant lock when nested locking is possible.
